title: How to version a spread property (ManagedServiceIdentityProperty)?

question: I'm trying to add Managed Identity support and want to avoid a breaking change.
 
However, adding `...Azure.ResourceManager.ManagedServiceIdentityProperty;` would update all my existing API versions and introduce a breaking change.
 
That's the right way to introduce the MSI property so I can only add it in a new version of my model?
 
If instead I'd directly add to my tracked resource `identity?: Foundations.ManagedServiceIdentity;` I get a warning about this not being valid in the resource envelope.

And how without having to create an entirely separate model. What I want is to introduce the property in a new API version `2025-05-04-preview` only.

ground_truth: You should use the @madeOptional decorator, here: [Decorators | TypeSpec](https://typespec.io/docs/libraries/versioning/reference/decorators/#@TypeSpec.Versioning.madeOptional).  Note that, making a property that occurs in responses optional is considered a breaking change.

From a purely "what is the TypeSpec syntax for assigning a default value to a type", no, I don't think we have any way of doing this. You can create a reusable property that you can spread into various places if that is what you are trying to accomplish.
 
From a service API design perspective, what actually changed between the API versions? The pending status was already there in older API versions. Presumably the property that had a type of ApprovalStatus always created things in a pending state (it looks like this is a type that would be used in a persisted model/resource). Wasn't that always conceptually pending? 
I think that shouldn't a problem on the breaking change part.

```
title: Changing interface's `update` from ArmResourcePatchAsync to ArmCustomPatchAsync without generating breaking changes

question:
Hi TypeSpec Discussion,

I am attempting to follow the playground example here TypeSpec Azure to get past a LintDiff error after adding an MSI to my resource. However, adding the new update model as well as changing the interface from update is ArmResourcePatchAsync<... to update is ArmCustomPatchAsync<... is generating breaking changes for older api versions.

Is there a way to only change the update is.. for the newest api version? I tried using the @added and @removed decorators but the interface complained about duplicate update.

Summary of answer:
To change the update operation from ArmResourcePatchAsync to ArmCustomPatchAsync without generating breaking changes for older API versions:

You also need to use @renamedFrom("update", newVersion) on the old update operation and put @sharedRoute on both.

Make sure you don’t use a model that is not available in a certain version and carry over the @added/@removed if needed.

If a property like userAssignedIdentities was marked as added in 2023, but the model it depends on (ManagedServiceIdentity) was only added later, it doesn’t make sense — this can be the result of composing shared models.

The sharedRoute might be sharing the new property to the old versions and not honoring the @added and @removed decorators.

If you mark the whole model like:

@added(Microsoft.Mission.Versions.v2024_06_01_preview)  
model ManagedServiceIdentityUpdate  

…errors may occur if parts of the model were added in older versions.

One workaround was to use ManagedServiceIdentityProperty instead of Azure.ResourceManager.Foundations.ManagedServiceIdentity

LintDiff errors like AvoidAnonymousTypes seem to be coming from the MSI additionalProperties section. This error wasn’t there before setting use-read-only-status-schema: true, but it’s unclear why that config causes it.

Warnings like "Use the latest version v5 of types.json" for old API versions or EnumInsteadOfBoolean for new ones can be ignored — warnings are not required to change for check-in, only errors.

False positives (like Avocado errors) may also occur when using @removed and @added in the same API version — especially for preview versions.

If everything is tagged properly and using the latest compiler version, you should be able to get it approved. After that, just follow the normal PR process (e.g., sign-offs, label like WaitForARMFeedback).
```
There is some documentation on this here: [Versioning | TypeSpec Azure](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/versioning/#converting-an-operation-from-synchronous-to-asynchronous) (this is for ARM, but the same principle applies)

query:
title: Handling multiple API versions using typespec

question: Hi Team,
 
I am releasing a new API version and looks there is a new validation to check existing swagger with new tsp file 
 
"appears to contain TypeSpec-generated swagger files, not generated from the current TypeSpec sources. Perhaps you deleted a version from your TypeSpec, but didn't delete the associated swaggers?"
 
We want to keep both old and new api versoins. What is the suggestion here? Do you suggest to create different TSP file for each version/use versioning in existing TSP? 
 
If second case, can you share some example where APIs/Properties are added/removed in a newer version
ground_truth:
The idea behind TypeSpec versioning is to model the diffs in your API, encouraging best practices for API evolution. If you have questions about modeling particular changes, feel free to ask.

About your concern: fixing a new validation causing changes to older APIs—this usually happens when new changes are added without using the appropriate version decorators. For example:

If you added properties or made a property optional, but didn’t annotate them with @added or @madeOptional, then they would apply to all versions by default, including older ones.

That’s likely why your stable version (e.g., 2024-12-01) got unintentionally updated when you only meant to target 2025-07-01-preview.

To avoid this, always use decorators like @added and @madeOptional to indicate version-specific changes.

The first question is:  are you relaxing this pattern across all api-versions in your service, or just the new api-version?
 
Generally speaking, patterns are not used by our client SDKs, and it is important for specs to be accurate to service behavior, so this kind of breaking change in the spec is generally allowed, if it really describes service behavior.
 
It is possible to do this, but it involves a remove/rename/replace pattern,  as in this playground.
 
The reason you have to do this is that in typespec, collections like Namespace or Model or Interface use the name of included types as their identifier, so you need two different names for these types.  In this case, you need two different model properties, and you cna use the renaming trick to remove and rename one and add the other in the version where the change is made, and ensure that the original property still has the correct name in previous versions.
 
However, if your service uses the new pattern across all api-versions, then it is best for your spec to reflect this.

it is generally better for review to isolate a change like this so it's easy to talk about it separately
using this `@removed/@renamedFrom` trick on the old operation, with `@added` on the new operation and  both using `@sharedRoute` works for this

query:
title: Composing resource types with different api versions for a new package.

question: We want to introduce a new resource type with a new api version, but do not want to change the api versions for any other resource types. Is it supported with typespec? Is documentation/example for this scenario?
ground_truth:
In TypeSpec Azure, it is NOT supported to introduce a new resource type with a new API version while keeping other resource types at their previous API versions within the same service namespace. The Azure guidelines require that all resources within a service (Resource Provider) share a single, unified API version at any given time. This means that when you add a new resource type, you must add a new API version for the entire service, and all resources (existing and new) are exposed under that new version.
This is enforced to ensure consistency for SDKs, tooling, and client experience. Mixing API versions for different resources within the same service is not allowed and is explicitly called out as a non-compliant pattern for TypeSpec Azure migration. If your service currently uses different API versions for different resources, you will need to plan for conformance—either by splitting the service (into multiple RPs) or by aligning all resources to a single API version.
There is no supported workaround or example for this scenario in TypeSpec Azure. The recommended approach is to add a new API version for the entire service when introducing a new resource type.
Note that this is not just typespec guidance, it is an SDK requirement.  For services composed of independent workgroups, there is al alternate mechanism, where each workgroup (or select workgroups) could publish their own sdks under different api-versions,  but this would not be a one-off, it would be a permanent architecture for service sdks.  There are also some exceptions for very good business cases - if you think you'd like to do one of these things, I would talk to the sdk onboarding folks.
 
Also note that here what is meant is that all resources currently active will be included in the latest api-version, but older api-versions will not be impacted by adding a new resource in new api-version.

query:
title: Introducing first GA version

question: Hey team, we are introducing the very first GA API version for our service, until now we have been under public preview, and we need some clarifications about the folder structure for the new GA version, specially to avoid breaking changes on the preview version.
 
Our current structure looks like:

```
orbital
└─ data-plane
   └─ Microsoft.PlanetaryComputer
      ├─ preview
      ├─ stable/2026-04-15
      └─ readme.md

Microsoft.PlanetaryComputer
├─ examples
├─ client.tsp
├─ inma.tsp
├─ main.tsp
├─ models.common.colormaps.tsp
├─ models.common.cql.tsp
...
```
So, under "/Microsoft.PlanetaryComputer" we added a new "/examples/2026-04-15" folder with the examples for the new version, we modified the Tsp for the GA version and generated a new OpenAI json in "/data-plane/Microsoft.PlanetaryComputer/2026-04-15"
 
We can see that during the PR the checks are also re-generating the 2025-04-30-preview version we are not sure how we can avoid such due we don't want to touch de preview version. Also we are not sure how the API Reference docs are going to be published for both versions. All help is appreciated.
ground_truth:
Short answer: for a **data-plane** TypeSpec service, your first GA should normally **replace** the active preview in TypeSpec rather than keep that same preview active. That is why your PR is likely still regenerating `2025-04-30-preview`: it is probably still present in `enum Versions` and/or still referenced by your README/config.

- **Correct emitted layout**
  - Generated OpenAPI should be under:
    - `data-plane/Microsoft.PlanetaryComputer/stable/2026-04-15/...`
    - not `data-plane/Microsoft.PlanetaryComputer/2026-04-15/...`
  - Your TypeSpec source files stay at the service root.

- **What to change for first GA**
  - Remove the old preview from `enum Versions`.
  - Rename `examples/2025-04-30-preview` to `examples/2026-04-15`.
  - Update every example’s `"api-version"` to `2026-04-15`.
  - Update `readme.md` to add the new stable version and make it the **default tag**.

```tsp
enum Versions {
  `2026-04-15`,
}
```

- **Why preview is still regenerating**
  - If `2025-04-30-preview` is still in TypeSpec, the compiler/checks will keep emitting it.
  - For data-plane, guidance is that preview should **not** remain active across stable releases.

- **If you still need preview-only features**
  - Don’t keep `2025-04-30-preview`.
  - Add a **newer** preview after GA, e.g.:
```tsp
enum Versions {
  `2026-04-15`,
  @Azure.Core.previewVersion
  `2026-07-01-preview`,
}
```

- **About docs publication**
  - Each service version has its own generated contract/docs surface.
  - Making `2026-04-15` the README default tag makes GA the default published/reference version.
  - If you continue to carry a preview version in README/generated outputs, it can remain separately visible.

- **Important nuance**
  - The TypeSpec guidance says if you want to delete the old preview OpenAPI files, do that in a **follow-up PR** after the GA PR merges. But the old preview should still be removed from the **active TypeSpec version enum** for the GA transition.

query:
title: Multiple preview versions

question: I see guidance for adding a preview version following a preview version, and it assumes that the new preview replaces the prior preview. However the prior preview is going to be made public, so it can't just "go away" with the replacement preview. What is the proper way to use the @previewVersion decorator in this case where the preview versions are both valid and will be public before a future stable version?
ground_truth:
For SDKs, the policy is to generate SDKs only for stable versions and the latest preview, which is why there is a 'single preview' policy in TypeSpec.  This also encourages conformance with Azure recommended retirement policies, and the maximum lifespan of a preview API.

Depending on why you want to have multiple active previews, the advice for the best way to proceed may be different:
- If there are multiple, independent teams that release different resources on different schedules, you may want to break your RP into multiple services, one for each working group, so that they can be versioned independently.  This would require a one-time breaking change in SDKs (assuming there are any GA SDKs).
- If you want to keep a new preview in private for development purposes, the right thing might be to have that version checked in to the private repo, and only move it to public when it replaces the previous preview.  Generally, check-ins to the public repo are only related to SDK releases.
- If you simply need the OpenAPI for RPaaS registration, API validation, or the like, you cnsa follow the advice for leaving the typespec-geenrated OpenAPI around for these purposes, while the typespec contains only the latest preview.

It is also possible to just have both preview versions in the spec, in which case the version is treated like any other version. (meaning that you can add and remove types relative to the previous version using versioning decorators) however, given the policies above, this runs afoul of the intended uses of TypeSpec in the public repo and policies.

query:
title: Swagger Avocado failure in new version rollout draft failure

question: We are deprecating 7 APIs as part of our recent work to remove triage workflow and rolling out new version which contains deprecation related changes. In new version folder, we have removed jsons for API we will be deprecating in examples folder, added @removed(Versions.v2026_03_01_preview) for deprecation in models.tsp and other related tsp as well. Locally tsp compile is working fine. After raising draft PR, I am seeing Swagger Avacado issue stating following error :
The default tag should contain all APIs. The API path
```
/subscriptions/{}/providers/microsoft.advisor/resiliencyreviews/{}/providers/microsoft.advisor/triagerecommendations
```
is not in the default tag. Please make sure the missing API swaggers are in the default tag.
readme: [resource-manager/Microsoft.Advisor/Advisor/readme.md](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/blob/d6c02eacbcc8f3370fc9342cdbbca09cb9bba393/specification/advisor/resource-manager/Microsoft.Advisor/Advisor/readme.md)
json: [Advisor/preview/2025-05-01-preview/openapi.json](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/blob/d6c02eacbcc8f3370fc9342cdbbca09cb9bba393/specification/advisor/resource-manager/Microsoft.Advisor/Advisor/preview/2025-05-01-preview/openapi.json)
 
Error is coming up for all 7 APIs we have removed JSONs. Need guidance on what should be next set of process to resolve this and roll out new version for API Dprecation.
ground_truth:
You are following the correct TypeSpec process for deprecating APIs: removing the example JSONs and marking the models and interfaces with @removed(Versions.v2026_03_01_preview). TypeSpec compiles fine, but Swagger Avocado is reporting errors that the default tag is missing the deprecated API paths. This is a known behavior of Avocado and the Azure REST API specs validation pipeline.
Why this happens:
Avocado expects all APIs present in previous versions to still exist in the new version unless they are properly versioned out. When you remove APIs (by marking them @removed and deleting their examples), the generated OpenAPI for the new version will not include those paths, which is correct.
However, Avocado's 'MISSING_APIS_IN_DEFAULT_TAG' check is not version-aware and will flag any removed APIs as missing, even if you followed the correct TypeSpec versioning/deprecation process.
What you should do:
1.Confirm you used @removed correctly:
Ensure all removed APIs (models, operations, interfaces) are decorated with @removed(Versions.v2026_03_01_preview) in your TypeSpec files. This tells the generator to exclude them from the new version's OpenAPI.
2.Breaking change review:
Removing APIs is a breaking change. You must go through the breaking change review process. Your PR will likely be flagged with 'BreakingChangeReviewRequired' or 'VersioningReviewRequired'. Follow the instructions in the PR comments and attend the required review meetings if needed.
3.Suppress Avocado errors (if needed):
For TypeSpec conversion and versioned API removal, Avocado errors like 'MISSING_APIS_IN_DEFAULT_TAG' can be suppressed by adding the label Approved-Avocado to your PR. This is an accepted practice for versioned API deprecation/removal when using TypeSpec, as Avocado does not fully support version-aware API removal yet.
See: "Avocado doesn't handle moves/renames. You can suppress by adding label Approved-Avocado."
4.Document the deprecation/removal:
In your PR description, clearly document which APIs are being removed, why, and reference the version in which they are removed. This helps reviewers and future maintainers.
5.Remove old preview versions if possible:
If the deprecated APIs were only in preview versions, you are encouraged to remove those old preview API versions from the specs repo once they are retired from the service.
Summary:
You are doing the right thing by using @removed and removing examples.
The Avocado error is expected and can be suppressed with the Approved-Avocado label after review.
Make sure to complete the breaking change review process.
If you need more details on the process, see the Azure TypeSpec versioning documentation and the Avocado known issues page.

query:
title: Need to change api model in new version in my service that is migrated to Typespec

question: Our service is migrated to TypeSpec and now i need to update the api model (add some new properties in the input and output) with new api version. what is the process to do all changes and raise PR?
ground_truth:
Do the work in two parts: (1) versioning changes in TypeSpec, and (2) repo/PR workflow.
1.Update the TypeSpec to add a new API version
In your main service namespace (the one with @versioned):
Add a new entry to your Versions enum for the new api-version.

```
@service({ title: "Contoso Widget Manager" })
@versioned(Contoso.WidgetManager.Versions)
namespace Contoso.WidgetManager;
enum Versions {
  v2022_08_31: "2022-08-31",
  v2022_11_30: "2022-11-30", // new version
}
```

If you are ARM, follow the ARM versioning guides (preview-after-stable, stable-after-stable, etc.) and ensure any preview versions are correctly marked with @Azure.Core.previewVersion.
Add/modify types using versioning decorators (do NOT copy-paste whole APIs per version):
To add new optional properties in the new version (recommended for non-breaking change):

```
model Widget {
  name: string;
  // New optional property available starting in v2022_11_30
  @added(Contoso.WidgetManager.Versions.v2022_11_30)
  color?: string;
}
```

To add a new required property or other changes, be aware these are breaking and will trigger the non-breaking-versioning rule. If the change is truly breaking, you may need a new API version and to coordinate with reviewers.
To add or change input/output shapes:
New input property: decorate that property on the request model with @added(Versions.<new>).
New output property: same pattern on the response model.
If you are changing an existing property (e.g., type, name, required/optional), use the appropriate decorators as in the versioning guide:
@madeOptional(Versions.vX) / @madeRequired(Versions.vX)
@renamedFrom(Versions.vX, "oldName")
@typeChangedFrom(Versions.vX, OldType) or @returnTypeChangedFrom for operations.
2.Update examples for the new version
Create a new examples folder for the new api-version by copying from the last version:
e.g. examples/2025-10-01 → examples/2026-01-01.
Update the api-version values inside all copied example JSONs to the new version string.
Adjust request/response bodies in examples to reflect the new properties (include new properties in the new version’s examples; omit them for older versions).
3.Compile and validate locally
From the repo root:

title: Breaking Change Review Help

question: I have made changes to some typespec models where I have added the annotation @removed on them for the new api version I have introduced. Now I am getting the "Breaking Change" label on my PR preventing it from getting reviewed. The RTs that are marked with @removed are not being used by the service/customers any more. So what is the guidance for proceeding with this scenario?
ground_truth:
You’re hitting the expected cross‑version breaking‑change checks (1005 RemovedPath, 1006 RemovedDefinition). Removing operations/models between GA API versions is a real breaking change from the tooling’s perspective, even if the service no longer uses them.
For management‑plane specs in the private repo, the correct way to proceed is:
1.Decide if this is truly a breaking change vs. a spec bug fix
If the old paths/RTs never worked as described (or have been non‑functional for their whole lifetime), you can treat the change as a bug fix to align spec with actual behavior.
If they were functional and customers could have used them, this is a real breaking change and must follow the formal Breaking Change process.
2.If it’s a spec bug fix (preferred when valid)
You may keep the new API version 2026‑03‑01 and:
Clearly document in the PR description that you are correcting the spec to match the actual service behavior and that the removed paths/models were never usable/never supported for customers.
Apply the label BreakingChange-Approved-BugFix yourself (PR authors are allowed to do this in this scenario).
Re‑run pipelines (/azp run). The BreakingChangeReviewRequired gating is then considered satisfied, and the PR can proceed to ARM review and normal approval.
3.If it’s a real breaking change (customers could have used those APIs)
You must go through the Azure Breaking Change process:
Follow the guidance at https://aka.ms/brch and the Azure Versioning and Breaking Changes Policy (aka.ms/AzBreakingChangesPolicy).
Submit a breaking‑change intake and obtain approval from the Breaking Change Review Board (and API board/SDK board if there’s SDK impact).
Once approved, the breaking‑change approver will apply Approved-BreakingChange (or guide you which approval label to use), which unblocks the PR.
4.About suppressions
For the Breaking Change(Cross-Version) check, there is no permanent suppression path documented; the supported route is policy/board approval plus an appropriate BreakingChange-* label, not a technical suppression in the spec.
So, in your concrete case:
If you can justify that schemaReferences / dynamicSchemas paths and their related RTs were never actually usable or supported, treat this as a bug‑fix, state that explicitly in the PR, and add BreakingChange-Approved-BugFix (and rerun checks).
If they were previously functional, you’ll need to file a breaking‑change proposal via aka.ms/brch, wait for approval, then proceed once an approver has applied the appropriate Approved-BreakingChange label.

query:
title: Updating a published preview Swagger

question: The preview version of our service has been published already, and we are working on adding the GA version. In the GA version, we have new routes and we wanted the users to use the new routes and not the ones in the preview version, so we applied the @deprecated decorator and regenerated the preview Swagger file along with the GA Swagger file. Now, the preview Swagger file has been updated to show the deprecated routes (with "deprecated": true on the affected operations). As the preview version is already published, is it acceptable to update the already-published preview Swagger file with these deprecation markers, or should the published preview Swagger remain unchanged? If we should not modify the published preview Swagger, what is the recommended approach to signal deprecation of preview routes when introducing a GA version?
ground_truth:
No — for a **publicly published** preview in `azure-rest-api-specs`, you should **not regenerate or edit that existing preview Swagger in place**, even just to add `deprecated: true`. The guidance says that once a GA or preview `api-version` is published to a production branch, you should **leave that version unchanged** and introduce a **newer dated api-version** instead.

**Recommended approach**
- **Keep the published preview Swagger as-is.**
- Publish the **new GA api-version** with the new routes.
- Treat the old preview as being **superseded** by the GA version; communicate that customers should migrate, and that the old preview can be retired after **90 days’ notice**.
- If you want an explicit runtime signal, use the service-side **`azure-deprecating` header** guidance rather than back-editing the old Swagger.
- After the preview version is **fully retired from the service**, remove its spec using the preview-retirement process.

query:
title: When using @added() on a required property

question: When using @added() on a required property, does TSP automatically make this property nullable on the models for older API versions?
ground_truth:
No. When you use @added() on a required property, TypeSpec does not retroactively change anything for older API versions.
Behavior is:
The property simply does not exist at all in versions before the @added version (it is neither required nor optional there).
Starting from the version you pass to @added, the property appears exactly as you declare it (required if you wrote prop: T;, optional if you wrote prop?: T;).
If you need a property to exist in all versions but change from required to optional (or vice versa), use @madeOptional / @madeRequired instead.

it's not entirely true that @added does nothing to previous versions.  If you add @added(Versions.v2)it makes the property not appear in versions before v2.  Other than the @removed decorator, all typespec versioning decorators fundamentally make changes on versions before the change  This is because the state of types in the spec most closely matches the latest version of the API.

query:
title: Typespec validation asking to delete previous generated swagger files

question: We are creating a new stable version following this doc: [Adding a Preview Version when the Last Version was Stable | TypeSpec Azure](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/versioning/04-preview-after-stable/) but I am getting this typespec validation error:  
 
 Output folder 'specification/billingbenefits/resource-manager/Microsoft.BillingBenefits' appears to contain TypeSpec-generated swagger files, not generated from the current TypeSpec sources. Perhaps you deleted a version from your TypeSpec, but didn't delete the associated swaggers?
  
  specification/billingbenefits/resource-manager/Microsoft.BillingBenefits/preview/2025-12-01-preview/billingbenefits.json
  specification/billingbenefits/resource-manager/Microsoft.BillingBenefits/preview/2026-02-01-preview/billingbenefits.json
  - Compiling...
  ✔ Compiling
  
  Error: TypeSpec Validation failed for project specification/billingbenefits/BillingBenefits.Management run the following command locally to validate.
 
We have some preview versions generated and customer will continue to use some of them so we could not delete them. Are we supposed to delete preview swagger when we are not generating this version from typespec anymore?
ground_truth:
From your change you are adding a new stable version and removing the old preview, so the document to follow is [Adding a Stable Version when the Last Version was Preview](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/versioning/03-stable-after-preview/#preparing-a-pr-into-the-azure-rest-api-specs-repo), not the preview-after-stable one.

You do not have to delete the old preview swagger. That validation error is not asking you to drop the versions your customers still use — it fires because the checked-in `billingbenefits.json` files still carry the `x-typespec-generated` marker in their `info` section while they are no longer emitted from the current TypeSpec sources (you removed those api-versions from the `Versions` enum), so TypeSpec Validation treats them as stale generated output.

Two options:

1. **You still need the old preview OpenAPI** — keep the files and remove the `x-typespec-generated` extension from the `info` section of each retained preview json:

   ```diff
     "info": {
       "title": "Microsoft.BillingBenefits management service",
       "version": "2025-12-01-preview",
   -   "description": "Microsoft.BillingBenefits Resource Provider management API.",
   -   "x-typespec-generated": [
   -     {
   -       "emitter": "@azure-tools/typespec-autorest"
   -     }
   -   ]
   +   "description": "Microsoft.BillingBenefits Resource Provider management API."
     },
   ```

   Once the extension is gone, validation stops treating those files as TypeSpec-generated and the error goes away.

2. **You don't need them** — delete the OpenAPI directory for those versions and remove every reference to them from `README.md`. Do this in a **separate follow-up PR** after the current PR merges, not in the same PR.

For ARM services it is safe to remove the swagger of an old api-version when any of these is true: the api-version is retired, the document is not needed for RPaaS live validation, or it is not needed for ARM registration. Until then, retain the file and use option 1. See "Should I Retain the OpenAPI for an Old Preview API (ARM Only)" in https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/versioning/01-about-versioning/ and the `x-typespec-generated` guidance in https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/versioning/uncommon-scenarios/02-perpetual-preview/

We have introduced new api-version to enhance the feature to support more functionalities in Microsoft.Edge\Configurations resource-type.
Existing model has just one readonly field - provisioningState till now in all existing api-versions - 2024-09-01-preview, 2025-06-01 and 2025-08-01.

New: [configurations/preview/2025-12-01-preview/configurations.json#L3295:7](https://github.com/patelkunal/azure-rest-api-specs-pr/blob/0af8181bd0735d27df24ea3a6f373680d59119a4/specification/edge/resource-manager/Microsoft.Edge/configurations/preview/2025-12-01-preview/configurations.json#L3295:7)

```

Although, it is based on customer input where customer selects if they want this then we will provision MRG via LRO operation. Otherwise, it is instantaneous sync response (200 status code). If this operation is synchronous in the previous stable version, then this change is a real breaking change that you will need to justify in breaking change review.

query:
title: Shall we include read-only properties in the PATCH schema?

question: Hi team, we have a question and appreciate some guidance:
With the current PATCH model, we noticed that read-only properties are not allowed in the PATCH request body. Should we define a custom PATCH model to allow users to include (i.e., copy over) read-only properties in the PATCH body?
What is the recommended user expectation in this scenario?

```
@patch(#{ implicitOptionality: true })
  update is ArmCustomPatchAsync<
    Policy,
    Azure.ResourceManager.Foundations.ResourceUpdateModel<
      Policy,
      PolicyProperties
>
>;
```
ground_truth: You should define a custom PATCH model, according to ARM guidelines, readOnly properties should not appear in the PATCH request body (although you can find lots of older services that do this, and if you are converting an older service, matching the previous PATCH request is ok)

No, it is NOT possible to append to a list property in a PATCH operation using Swagger (OpenAPI) or TypeSpec for Azure Resource Manager (ARM) resource providers. According to Azure API guidelines and ARM RPC rules, PATCH operations must follow the JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) semantics. This means that when you PATCH an array property, the value you provide will REPLACE the existing array, not append to it.
If you PATCH a property like `myList: [1,2,3]`, the resource's `myList` will become exactly `[1,2,3]`, regardless of its previous value. There is no standard or ARM-compliant way to specify 'append' semantics for arrays in PATCH requests. This is by design to ensure predictability and consistency across all Azure RPs.
If you need to support append-like behavior, you must implement a custom POST action (not PATCH) that takes the value to append and performs the append server-side. However, this is not standard for resource PATCH and should only be used for resource actions, not for the main PATCH operation.
Your current usage of `ArmResourceCreateOrReplaceSync` for PUT and `ArmResourcePatchSync` for PATCH is correct and compliant. PATCH will always replace the array property if it is provided in the request body.

Just to be clear, for the rp-specific property bag of a resource, you should abide by rules for `application/merge-patch+json`,  which means that, if the user specifies an array property in the PATCH request, it replaces the existing values in the array.  If you'd like to have an operation that appends values to a resource array, this would have to be a separate resource action.

query:
title: Does it make sense for a put operation with Location header?

question: This is an [example](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/blob/5f272067844826380939c0b3f24ca3cc99dbe308/specification/storage/resource-manager/Microsoft.Storage/stable/2024-01-01/storageTaskAssignments.json#L60-L92). ground_truth:
For everyone on the channel,  such an operation doesn't make sense.  No one should write an ARM put operation that returns a 202, it is in violation of the ARM RPC.
 
I believe that you are talking about how to model an existing brownfield operation that violates the RPC without breaking.
 
Yes, it is possible to do this, as in this playground.  But this should only be done in a brownfield conversion to prevent breaking changes to the API.  You should also be completely sure that your API actually behaves this way - client SDKs can be very flexible in resolving lros, and the flexibility of the SDKs may hide an error in your api specification
The current lro mechanism is designed to allow multiple pathways to resolve the lro, and to select one as the 'favored pathway' for clients - in general we should describe what the service does and make sure that we give our clients the right information.
 
We will be working on standardizing what new services do.

For a brownfield conversion, model the non-compliant PUT (202 + `Location` header) with a custom create operation and suppress the response-codes rule:

```typespec
@armResourceOperations
interface Employees {
  /** Create an employee */
  #suppress "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-resource-manager/arm-put-operation-response-codes"
  @armResourceCreateOrUpdate(Employee)
  @put
  createOrUpdate is Azure.ResourceManager.Foundations.ArmCreateOperation<
    ResourceInstanceParameters<
      Employee,
      Azure.ResourceManager.Foundations.DefaultBaseParameters<Employee>
    >,
    Employee,
    ArmAcceptedLroResponse<LroHeaders = ArmAsyncOperationHeader<FinalResult = Employee> &
      ArmLroLocationHeader<FinalResult = Employee> &
      Azure.Core.Foundations.RetryAfterHeader>,
    ErrorResponse
  >;
}
```

query:
title: LRO header return 200

question: Hi, I'm from the servicefabric RP team working with [azure-rest-api-specs/specification/servicefabricmanagedclusters/resource-manager/Microsoft.ServiceF…](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/blob/main/specification/servicefabricmanagedclusters/resource-manager/Microsoft.ServiceFabric/ServiceFabricManagedClusters/preview/2025-06-01-preview/servicefabricmanagedclusters.json)
On our operations for ManagedClusters_CreateOrUpdate, NodeTypes_CreateOrUpdate, and ApplicationTypeVersions_CreateOrUpdate, we have both a 200 and 202 response defined.
A 200 response is returned when the customer sends the initial request to create the resource. A 202 is returned on every subsequent PUT.
I recently noticed that our service code returns an async operation URI in the 200 response for the above operations. https://msazure.visualstudio.com/One/_git/winfab-RP?path=/src/sfmc/SfmcBackendService/Service/Controllers/ClustersController.cs&version=GBdevelop&line=294&lineEnd=295&lineStartColumn=1&lineEndColumn=1&lineStyle=plain&_a=contents
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-length: 2131
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Server: Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0
Azure-AsyncOperation: http://localhost:8080/subscriptions/b36cdf46-b75d-4dc2-9fe1-1296ee8c623d/providers/Microsoft.ServiceFabric/locations/southcentralus/managedclusteroperations/c39cd8e1-18a0-41fc-a778-6a4ad6adbd653?api-version=2024-02-01
Date: Thu, 23 Oct 2025 22:57:10 GMT
Connection: close
```
Should I specify this in the spec? If so, what is the recommendation for doing so? I couldn't find an example for a 200 response with an async operation header.
ground_truth:
Based on ARM RPC guidelines and the TypeSpec ARM templates:
1.You generally should NOT model “subsequent PUT returns 202” for a resource PUT.
For ARM resource PUT, the required pattern is: return `201` for create and `200` for update, and if the operation is long-running you still use `x-ms-long-running-operation: true` and include the appropriate LRO headers.
Returning `202` for PUT is explicitly called out as an old model and is no longer supported for new resource types/patterns.
2.If your service returns an async polling header on the `200` response, it’s OK (and often desirable) to specify it — but only if the operation is actually long-running in that case.
In ARM, the LRO “polling” header is typically `Azure-AsyncOperation` (required for greenfield starting Jan 2025 per RPC contract) and/or `Location` (required for 202 patterns; also commonly used).
For PUT LROs, the standard ARM templates already model the correct behavior: `200` and `201` responses with the resource body, and LRO headers on the create response (and depending on template/pattern, can be present when the operation is async).
3.Recommended way to model this in TypeSpec (preferred over hand-authoring swagger)
Use the ARM operation template for async PUT, and let the emitter generate the correct OpenAPI, including `x-ms-long-running-operation-options.final-state-via`.
If you need `Azure-AsyncOperation` to be the final-state mechanism, use the template that emits that (e.g. `ArmResourceCreateOrUpdateAsync` / `ArmResourceCreateOrReplaceAsync` depending on your chosen semantics).
Example (management-plane, ARM):
```
import "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-resource-manager";
using Azure.ResourceManager;
@armResourceOperations
interface ManagedClusters {
// Pick the template that matches your service’s LRO header behavior.
// This produces 200/201 + x-ms-long-running-operation and final-state-via azure-async-operation.
createOrUpdate is ArmResourceCreateOrReplaceAsync<ManagedCluster>;
}
```
4.If you truly must keep a 202-on-PUT behavior (brownfield), align it to ARM guidance rather than just documenting the current behavior.
The guidance is to fix the service to return `200/201` for PUT (even when async) and rely on LRO headers + provisioningState.
If you cannot change runtime behavior immediately, you should discuss with ARM/API review because it conflicts with the current ARM contract guidance for PUT.
5.About “200 response with async operation header” specifically
In OpenAPI/Swagger, you can absolutely define headers on the `200` response. There’s nothing structurally preventing it.
However, the recommended ARM modeling is to use the standard templates so the LRO metadata is consistent (headers + `x-ms-long-running-operation` + `final-state-via`). Don’t invent a one-off pattern unless you have to.
If you paste the relevant snippet of your current swagger responses for one of these PUTs (the `responses` block), I can tell you exactly what to change and which TypeSpec template/parameters best match your service behavior (including whether you should be using `ArmResourceCreateOrReplaceAsync` vs `ArmResourceCreateOrUpdateAsync`, and whether you need `Location` and/or `Azure-AsyncOperation`).

title: @secret in POST operation response

question: Hi,
We have a property returned by a POST operation response that was required by validation to use `@secret` this returns values user needs to use in their application to use certain feature of our service.  Since the values are sensitive we return it as response of a POST action and not in any GET response. This I belive is in compliance with the RPC
Just to clarify, can /will this value be masked/sanitized in API POST response or generated SDKs ?
ground_truth:
If you decorate a property with @secret in TypeSpec, this does NOT mean the value will be masked or sanitized in the API POST response or in generated SDKs. The @secret decorator is used to indicate that the property contains sensitive information (such as passwords, keys, tokens, credentials, or other secrets) and is required by Azure ARM guidelines for proper identification and handling of secrets.
The actual value will be returned in the POST response as specified by your API contract. The @secret decorator ensures that the property is marked as sensitive in the OpenAPI spec (via x-ms-secret), which informs tooling, SDKs, and Azure services to treat it with extra care (e.g., not logging it, not exposing it in GET responses, and possibly prompting SDKs to handle it securely). However, it does NOT automatically mask or sanitize the value in the response payload.
Your approach—returning the secret only in the POST response and not in GET responses—is fully compliant with Azure API guidelines. If you want to mask or sanitize the value, you must implement that logic in your service backend. TypeSpec and the generated OpenAPI/SDKs will not do this automatically.

query:
title: Patch for readonly properties for service

question: Just like provisioning state which has the lifecycle. Read visibility decorator, if we have properties that have that decorator, can they be calculated and patched by the service alone ?
ground_truth:
Properties decorated with @visibility(Lifecycle.Read) are intended to be read-only from the client's perspective—they are only included in responses (such as GET, PUT, PATCH, or LIST), and are not expected to be provided by the client in create or update requests. These properties are typically calculated or set by the service itself, similar to how 'provisioningState' is handled in ARM resources.
However, such properties should NOT be patched (i.e., updated) by the client. The service is responsible for setting or updating these values internally. If a client attempts to send a value for a property marked with @visibility(Lifecycle.Read) in a PATCH or PUT request, the service should ignore it or reject the request, treating it as a read-only field. This is consistent with Azure API guidelines and ARM patterns, where properties like 'provisioningState' are managed by the service and not settable by the client.
In summary: Properties with @visibility(Lifecycle.Read) are calculated and managed by the service, not patched or set by the client.

        "Succeeded"
      ],
      "x-ms-enum": {

            "value": "Failed",

            "value": "Succeeded",

ground_truth:
You cannot make the LinkStatus enum schema itself readOnly: true via TypeSpec today in the same way OperationStatusEnum is handled.
What you are seeing is a special-purpose workaround, not general behavior:
The readOnly on OperationStatusEnum is produced by the @azure-tools/typespec-autorest option use-read-only-status-schema: true.
That option only targets status-like types (e.g. ProvisioningState, "operation status") to work around the ProvisioningStateMustBeReadOnly validator issue; it is not a generic mechanism for marking arbitrary enums as read-only.
TypeSpec itself can only express read-only semantics on properties, via lifecycle visibility, e.g.

```
model ConnectionProperties {
  @visibility(Lifecycle.Read)
  linkStatus: LinkStatus;
}
```

This correctly becomes a read-only property in OpenAPI:

```
"linkStatus": {
  "$ref": "#/definitions/LinkStatus",
  "readOnly": true
}
```

But there is currently no supported decorator to put readOnly: true on the LinkStatus schema itself, and the ARM/Autorest toolchain does not rely on readOnly at the schema level for enforcement.

Your TypeSpec is already expressing the intended read-only semantics correctly.
The fact that the private RP allows clients to send linkStatus is a service implementation issue, not something you can fix from TypeSpec/OpenAPI alone.

Recommended actions:
1.Keep linkStatus as a read-only property:

```
@visibility(Lifecycle.Read)
linkStatus: LinkStatus;
```

2.Ensure the RP implementation ignores / rejects linkStatus on create/update requests.
3.Do not depend on having readOnly: true on the LinkStatus enum schema; this is not required by Azure guidelines and is not generally supported by TypeSpec.
If you need a general, explicit way to mark an enum schema as read-only in the future, this would require a new emitter feature (e.g. a decorator like @readOnlySchema) in @azure-tools/typespec-autorest; today that does not exist.

title: What does @identifiers (in Azure.ResourceManager) actually do?

question: What does @identifiers (in Azure.ResourceManager) actually do? Are there side effects, uniqueness constraints, etc?
ground_truth:
In Azure.ResourceManager, @identifiers is purely descriptive metadata used to tell tooling which properties in an array element type are treated as the element’s identifiers. It:
Is applied on an array-typed model property: @identifiers(#["prop1", "prop2"]) items: ItemModel[];
Causes the ARM emitter to generate x-ms-identifiers on that array property in the OpenAPI (or equivalent metadata for other emitters).
It does not by itself:
Enforce runtime or compile-time uniqueness of those properties
Add validation that the values are unique in the array
Change required/optional status of the properties
Change wire format or API behavior beyond the x-ms-identifiers annotation
Any uniqueness or business rules around those identifiers must be enforced by the service or separate validation logic; @identifiers just marks which fields should be considered identifiers for that array element type by ARM and client tooling.

Unfortunately, TypeSpec does not currently support versioned default values for required fields. If you want to assign a default value to a required field, you'll need to use the "remove/rename dance" workaround shown in the referenced playground: remove the old field and reintroduce it with a default value. It is not ideal, but it is currently the only way.

title: Should I add a visibilityFilter to a model

question: Should I add a visibilityFilter to a model so that all properties are only visible on Read when the model is only being used as a return result of an operation, or is that implicit?
ground_truth:
ou do not need to explicitly add a visibilityFilter or use @withVisibility(Lifecycle.Read) if your model is only used as the return result of an operation. TypeSpec's HTTP library and standard emitters automatically apply Lifecycle.Read visibility to properties when a model is used as a return type. By default, properties are included in the response if they have Lifecycle.Read visibility, and all properties have all visibilities enabled unless you restrict them with @visibility.
Therefore, unless you have properties with more restrictive visibilities, all properties will be included in the response by default. If you want to limit which properties are returned, you should annotate those properties with @visibility(Lifecycle.Read) or other appropriate modifiers, but you do not need to explicitly use a visibilityFilter just because a model is a response type.
If you use the built-in Lifecycle visibility model as intended, the behavior you expect is implicit and handled automatically for response models.

title: Is adding new value to enum is considered a breaking change?

question: Hi Team,
 
We are working on Workload Orchestration Service which is going to GA soon. In swagger, we have data models where we have enum defined as

```
union State {
  InReview: "InReview",
  UpgradeInReview: "UpgradeInReview",
  ReadyToDeploy: "ReadyToDeploy",
  ReadyToUpgrade: "ReadyToUpgrade",
  Deploying: "Deploying",
  Deployed: "Deployed",
  Failed: "Failed",
  Undeployed: "Undeployed",
  PendingExternalValidation: "PendingExternalValidation",
  ExternalValidationFailed: "ExternalValidationFailed",
  Staging: "Staging",
  string,
}

model SolutionProperties {
  resourceState: State
}
```
In future, if we add new value to this existing enums in same api-version after GA, then will it be considered as breaking change or not? Will it cause any failure anywhere in swagger, SDK, etc?
ground_truth:
extensible union as defined in your example wouldn't count as a breaking change to add a new entry as it defines this as already allowing any string
For clarity,  an 'extensible enum'  is represented in TypeSpec as an open union.  That is a union of string values that include string as a variant (`union Foo { Bar: "bar", Baz: "baz", string}`).  In this case, adding new values is not a breaking change, but removing values is
 
An enum or closed union (union with just literal string variants, `union Foo {Bar: "bar", Baz: "baz"}`) is considered a closed enum, which means that adding or removing values is a breaking change.
 
The reason for the difference is that some SDKs have enumeration types that are used when an enum is comprehensive (closed),  but not used if the enum is partial.  When the enumeration types are used, customer code can break if it processes each of the variants explicitly.
 
This is why we highly recommend use open enumerations in most cases, and to use a closed enum you have to suppress a linting rule.

title: Go SDK prevents union discriminator?

question: I'm reviewing a Typespec PR that includes this suppression: 
```
#suppress "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-core/no-string-discriminator" "Discriminator must be plain string for cross-language SDK compatibility (Go emitter does not support extensible unions as discriminator values)."
```
Is this true?
ground_truth:
The justification in that suppression is not accurate, and you should not rely on it.
Azure guidance explicitly prefers extensible unions for discriminators and has a dedicated rule (no-string-discriminator) to enforce this. That rule exists precisely to avoid using a plain string as the discriminator type, so suppressing it on the grounds of SDK compatibility is going against current Azure TypeSpec guidance.
Current Azure client emitters (including Go) are designed to work with the standard @discriminator pattern, and the Azure docs show the discriminator both as a plain string and as an extensible union. There is no official guidance saying that the Go emitter cannot handle extensible unions as discriminator values; on the contrary, the guidance is to use them so adding new discriminator values is non‑breaking.
Therefore:
The statement "Go emitter does not support extensible unions as discriminator values" should not be treated as a general truth or as a standing reason to bypass the rule.
The preferred fix is to change the discriminator property to an extensible union (open enum) rather than suppressing the rule. Only if you hit a concrete, currently-unfixable emitter bug (with a linked issue) should you consider suppression, and then the reason should clearly reference that specific bug rather than a broad claim about Go support.
So: the suppression as written is not well justified and, in normal circumstances, is not necessary. The model should be updated to use an extensible union discriminator instead of a plain string.

Swagger copy: https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/tree/33737ff460f78153f4cc21ef5d2d4586fcbae107/specification/containerservice/resource-manager/Microsoft.ContainerService/fleet/preview/2025-07-01-preview/examples
 
TypeSpec copy: https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/tree/33737ff460f78153f4cc21ef5d2d4586fcbae107/specification/containerservice/Fleet.Management/examples/2025-07-01-preview
 
Process is you update examples in TypeSpec copy, then run "tsp compile" which copies them to swagger folder
 
Your TSV may have been failing, if you changed one copy but not the other
 
Second, you can generate examples manually or using `oav` , whatever you prefer, is more efficient for your workflow, etc
 
If you think you're hitting a bug in `oav`, you can open an issue here, or discuss in any of our teams channels.
 
https://github.com/Azure/oav/issues

For Problem 1,  The 'title' field in the example file determines the name of the example in the 'x-ms-examples' extension, file names have nothing to do with it.  TypeSpec and tsv have no preference for the names of example files, as long as they are in the configured example directory.  It is possible, however, for an example to be dropped if it shares the same 'title'  and 'operation Id'  with another example file.
For Problem 2, oav generate-examples is a best-effort tool to help you get started generating examples from Swagger.  You may need to further edit the examples after generation.
For Problem 3, The source of truth for your examples, is the "examples" folder alongside your TSP sources.  tsp compile copies these examples alongside your generated swagger.
For Problem 4,  'location' is required in any tracked resource, so a set of values with one resource would have this property.

query:
title: How to create an Example for a typespec model?

question: I was going through my Typespec file and adding @example() decorators on top of models but then I was informed that Azure API Spec doesn't support the @example() decorator? Instead I'm supposed to create .json files in the examples folder and link it by operaiton id. However, models don't have operation ids? or do they?
ground_truth:
Here is some documentation on generating required examples: [x-ms-examples example files | TypeSpec Azure](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/migrate-swagger/faq/x-ms-examples/).  
Note that the examples that are required for specs at this point are operation examples (which include examples of model serialization in the operations that include those models).  The workflow is:
Design your API in TypeSpec
Generate an OpenApi doc by compiling your spec
Run oav to generate examples for each of the operations (oav generates syntactically valid examples with the 'operationId'  and 'title' fields filled in)
Go through the examples, replace values to make the examples more useful as documentation, and feel free to add  any examples for important scenarios that might be difficult to understand otherwise, or remove redundant examples (although you will need at least one per operation)
Copy the examples into the `examples/<api-version>/` folder inside your typespec directory and the OpenApi emitter will automatically associate the examples with  the appropriate operatiosn through the 'operationId' in the example file,  using the 'title' field as the title of the example.

query:
title: npx tsv auto deleting examples from swagger

question: npx tsv is auto deleting our examples from swagger. We ran validate-example command and validation passes correctly.
```
c:\azurecompute\azure-rest-api-specs\specification\azurefleet\resource-manager\Microsoft.AzureFleet\AzureFleet>oav validate-example "c:\azurecompute\azure-rest-api-specs\specification\azurefleet\resource-manager\Microsoft.AzureFleet\AzureFleet\preview\2026-04-01-preview\azurefleet.json"
{
  message: validating examples under "c:\azurecompute\azure-rest-api-specs\specification\azurefleet\resource-manager\Microsoft.AzureFleet\AzureFleet\preview\2026-04-01-preview\..."
  level: "\x18[32minfo\x18[39m'
}
Validation completes without errors.
```
But when npx tsv is run locally, examples are being deleted from swagger. How do we fix this? We checked that the generated names are correct in the example files.
 

Could someone help how to fix this? We compiled first, generated examples, validated examples, ran npx tsv again - This is when all examples get deleted from generated swagger.
 
This is causing typespec validation to fail on the PR.
ground_truth:
This happens when tsv (via tsp compile) doesn’t see any examples at the TypeSpec source location, so the emitter regenerates the Swagger without any x-ms-examples, effectively deleting all examples in the generated OpenAPI.
For Azure REST specs using TypeSpec, the source of truth for examples is not the Swagger folder; it is the examples/<api-version>/ folder located next to your TypeSpec project. tsp compile then copies those example files into the Swagger folder and wires them up in x-ms-examples.
In your case, you:
1.Compiled TypeSpec → generated Swagger.
2.Ran oav generate-examples directly against the Swagger (or otherwise created examples only under the Swagger path).
3.Ran npx tsv again → tsv recompiled the TypeSpec and overwrote the Swagger, but since the examples weren’t present under the TypeSpec examples source folder, they were dropped.
To fix this and get TypeSpec validation passing:
1.Identify your TypeSpec examples source folder for AzureFleet, something like:
specification/azurefleet/AzureFleet.Management/examples/2026-04-01-preview (exact path depends on your project layout, but it will be under the TypeSpec project root, not under resource-manager/.../preview/.../examples).
2.Move/copy your example JSON files into that TypeSpec examples folder. If you generated them with oav from the Swagger folder, copy them from:
specification/azurefleet/resource-manager/Microsoft.AzureFleet/AzureFleet/preview/2026-04-01-preview/examples/ to the corresponding TypeSpec examples folder.
3.Ensure each example file has:
A unique and descriptive title per operation.
The correct operationId matching the operation in your TypeSpec/OpenAPI (you said you already verified this, which is good).
4.Run the standard sequence from the repo root:
```
git clean -xdf   # beware: removes local changes not committed
git pull
npm ci
npx tsv specification/azurefleet/AzureFleet.Management
```
This will:
Compile TypeSpec,
Copy examples from the TypeSpec examples folder to the Swagger folder,
Regenerate azurefleet.json with x-ms-examples wired to those files.
5.Check git status; the only diffs in swagger should be the intended ones. If examples are still missing, double‑check that:
The TypeSpec tspconfig.yaml for AzureFleet is configured with the correct examples directory (follow the Widget sample’s pattern), and
There are no duplicate title + operationId pairs between files (duplicates can cause examples to be dropped).

Once the examples live in the correct TypeSpec source folder and tsp compile manages them, npx tsv will stop deleting them and TypeSpec validation should pass.

query:
title: Customizing key for child operation

question: Is there a way to customize the key of a parent resource for a specific child operation?
 
In SDKs we are being asked to change the name, but I couldn't find a good place to apply the `@clientName` decorator.
ground_truth:
In the data plane API, resource keys are typically derived from the parent resource’s key and are not individually specified for each operation. By default, the key names for operations are inherited from the parent resource's key. The @clientName decorator is used to modify the name used by the client, not to change the parent resource's key in operations. To change the parent resource's key name globally, the simplest solution is to use the @key decorator on the name property to ensure consistency.

Changing the key name specifically for certain operations is not straightforward because operation keys are typically tied to the parent resource key. Although you can explicitly define different keys for an operation, this generally requires redefining the operation.

In your case, the most reasonable approach would be to update the parent resource's key name to jobName across all operations to maintain consistency rather than using a different name for some operations. This approach reduces naming conflicts and ensures consistency.

For how to explicitly specify key definitions, you can refer to the Azure Data Plane documentation, which outlines how to define keys for each service's operations and resources.

query:
title: Is it so bad to introduce named types to replace unnamed ones?

question: I notice a suppression in the typespec PR 
 
#suppress "@azure-tools/typespec-client-generator-core/no-unnamed-types" "Backwards compatibility with existing clients."
 
Sounds like the PR author is under the impression its a bad idea to get rid of unnamed types and replace them with named ones, because of concerns about backwards compatibility. Is this actually correct?
 
Or would we consider this a benign change? And a best practice to 'fix' unnamed types by creating named types to replace them?
ground_truth:
Introducing named types to replace unnamed ones is not a bad idea—in fact, it's preferred. The linter rule @azure-tools/typespec-client-generator-core/no-unnamed-types exists to encourage naming types. However, in the PR you referenced, there was a suppression added with the justification of "Backwards compatibility with existing clients."

After reviewing the context, it seems this suppression may not be necessary. The rule itself is currently disabled due to performance issues, so removing the suppression won’t trigger CI. Conceptually, this is a false positive: the anonymous model created via @bodyRoot is a temporary structure that the SDK won’t use, so it shouldn't be flagged.

Still, the current template resolves to a borderline case where the SDK might auto-generate a name. A cleaner approach would be to use @@clientName to rename the body parameter directly, avoiding the anonymous model altogether. This is considered a better practice.

So yes—replacing unnamed types with named ones is generally a good idea, and in this case, the suppression may not be needed.

query:
title: FlattenProperty on discriminated unions

question: We have a TypeSpec model where a resource Job has a properties field that is a discriminated union (JobProeprties, with subtypes CommandJob, SweepJob, etc.):
```
model Job {
  name: string;
  properties: JobProperties;  // discriminated union
}

@discriminator("jobType")
model JobProperties { ... }

model CommandJob extends JobProperties { ... }
model SweepJob extends JobProperties { ... }
```

Currently customers must unwrap the envelope and cast:

```
result = client.jobs.get(name="my-job")
props = cast(CommandJob, result.properties)
```

We want customers to work with a flat object directly:

```
result = client.jobs.get(name="my-job")
result.command   # no unwrapping, no cast
```
We explored [flattenProperty](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/libraries/typespec-client-generator-core/reference/decorators/#@Azure.ClientGenerator.Core.Legacy.flattenProperty) but it is explicitly blocked on discriminated unions.
 
Question: Is there any TypeSpec decorator or emitter customization that achieves flattening of a discriminated union property without writing per-language custom patch code?
ground_truth:
There is currently no supported way in TypeSpec + Azure emitters to flatten a discriminated-union properties field the way you describe, without per‑language customization.
Key points:
1.`@Azure.ClientGenerator.Core.Legacy.flattenProperty` is the only flattening decorator for Azure client generation, and it is:
Marked as legacy and not recommended for new (green‑field) services.
Designed for simple model properties; it does not support discriminated unions or polymorphic envelopes.
`@Azure.ClientGenerator.Core.Legacy.flattenProperty(scope?: valueof string)`
2.Azure’s current guidance for polymorphism is to use `@discriminator` on a base model and generate normal polymorphic clients, not to auto‑flatten the discriminated property into the parent model’s surface.
3.There is no other Azure or core TypeSpec decorator (e.g., `@alternateType`, `@discriminated`, etc.) that will:
Keep the wire format as `Job { properties: JobProperties }`, and
Automatically project `properties`’s discriminated variants as flattened members like result.command in all client SDKs.
`@alternateType` can change the exposed client type, but not in a way that generically flattens a polymorphic union into the parent model across languages, and it is not intended for this scenario.
4.To change the SDK surface to something like `result.command` without manual patching, you would need to change the TypeSpec shape (and therefore the wire contract), e.g.:
Model `Job` itself as a polymorphic resource (`@discriminator` on `Job` and have `CommandJob extends Job`, `SweepJob extends Job`), or
Introduce non‑polymorphic top‑level properties on `Job` and stop using an envelope `properties` union.
Both are breaking changes and must be evaluated against your API versioning strategy.
So, with the current Azure TypeSpec toolchain:
You cannot use a decorator to transparently flatten a discriminated‑union `properties` field into `Job`.
Achieving that experience requires either (a) client‑side customization per language, or (b) a redesign of the TypeSpec model/wire contract (e.g., polymorphic `Job` instead of polymorphic `Job.properties`).

query:
title: Question on TypeSpec Settings for Constructor Visibility in SDK Generation

question: could you help clarify which Typespec settings control whether properties are generated with a public constructor or an internal constructor in the SDK? Thanks!

ground_truth:
The Python signature is intentionally using None instead of the TypeSpec default, and there isn’t a supported way to change that behavior today.
TypeSpec defaults (like force?: boolean = false) are defined as service‑side defaults. The core TypeSpec guidance is that emitters must not turn those into client‑side defaults in SDKs; they should be used by the service implementation when the client omits the value, and reflected in documentation instead of in the client method’s default argument. This is called out explicitly in the emitter docs:
default values are accessed via modelProp.default in emitters
they “SHOULD NOT be used as client-side default values”
they “SHOULD be expressed in documentation to properly communicate the server-side default”
The Python generator follows this rule by:
making the parameter optional (Optional[bool])
using None as the default so the client can distinguish “not passed” from an explicit value
leaving the service default to be communicated through docs rather than via the function signature.
For brownfield cases where an SDK must expose a client‑side default (e.g., to preserve behavior after moving from Swagger to TypeSpec), there is a legacy escape hatch: @Azure.ClientGenerator.Core.Legacy.clientDefaultValue. This is specifically documented as legacy and for backward compatibility, not for new services.
So for a new Foundry data-plane API, the recommended and supported pattern is:
Keep force?: boolean = false in TypeSpec as the service default
Let the emitted Python method use force: Optional[bool] = None
Clearly document in the parameter docstring that the service default is false when omitted.
There isn’t a configuration switch in the current Python emitter to automatically generate force: Optional[bool] = False from the TypeSpec default. Doing so would violate the shared emitter guidance and could also create ambiguity between “unspecified” and “explicitly false” at the client layer.

Add
@@Azure.ClientGenerator.Core.Legacy.flattenProperty(ArcSettings.propeties)
By convention put this in a back-compatible.tsp file.

query: title: RT registration for Type Spec folder with multiple swagger files question: Hello Team, We added a [new RT ScimApiConsumption](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs-pr/tree/chiragm28/entraScim/specification/identitygovernance/resource-manager/Microsoft.EntraidGovernance/ScimApiConsumption/preview/2025-10-17-preview) under an existing RP namespace Microsoft.EntraIDGovernance. The new folder structure is something like ``` resource-manager --> Microsoft.EntraidGovernance ----> ScimApiConsumption (New folder for NEW RT) ------> preview/2025-10-17-preview --------> examples --------> scimopenapi.json ----> preview/2025-06-13-preview (existing folder) --------> examples --------> openapi.json ``` I have the following questions 1.The existing RT registration uses the swagger path ``` "azure-rest-api-specs-pr/tree/RPSaaSMaster/specification/identitygovernance/resource-manager/Microsoft.EntraidGovernance/" ``` Will the new folder structure have an impact because of presence of multiple swagger files? Will we have to update the swagger path to point to ``` "azure-rest-api-specs-pr/tree/RPSaaSMaster/specification/identitygovernance/resource-manager/Microsoft.EntraidGovernance/preview" ``` 2.Similarly, for the new RT registration should we pass the swagger path scoped to associated swagger file? i.e. ``` "azure-rest-api-specs-pr/tree/RPSaaSMaster/specification/identitygovernance/resource-manager/Microsoft.EntraidGovernance/ScimApiConsumption" ```
ground_truth:
First clarify the intent: is ScimApiConsumption supposed to be a different service from the APIs that sit in Microsoft.EntraidGovernance/preview, i.e. will it ship its own set of SDKs, have its own versioning lifecycle, and be relatively independent from the existing APIs in customer scenarios?

1. If yes, you should add a new service folder parallel with ScimApiConsumption and move the APIs currently under the Microsoft.EntraidGovernance/preview folder into that new folder, so the layout is aligned with the [new folder structure guideline](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Azure-Service-Versioning-Guideline#an-azure-resource-provider-and-its-1-azure-services). That guideline requires:
   - An RP namespace itself contains no code and never versions. It can contain 1+ control-plane services and 0+ data-plane services, and an Azure service is "a set of operations that version uniformly (in perpetuity)", with each service version getting its own API contract, documentation and SDK package.
   - The expected repo layout is `specification/<orgName>/resource-manager/<RPNamespace>/<ServiceName>/`, where `<ServiceName>` is the customer-facing service name. The `<ServiceName>` folder must contain only `readme.*`, `tspconfig.yaml` and `*.tsp` files, plus an `examples/` subfolder (one subfolder per api-version, example `*.json` files only) and `preview/` and `stable/` subfolders. Additional subfolders are allowed only to help organize `*.tsp` files.
   - The compiled OpenAPI must therefore live in `<ServiceName>/preview/YYYY-MM-DD-preview/` or `<ServiceName>/stable/YYYY-MM-DD/`, each with its own `examples/` folder. So an api-version folder such as `Microsoft.EntraidGovernance/preview/2025-06-13-preview` hanging directly off the RP namespace folder does not follow the structure - that content belongs in its own service folder next to ScimApiConsumption.
   - For an RPaaS service there must be exactly one `readme.md` in the `resource-manager` folder and 1+ service-name folders under `resource-manager/<RPNamespace>`, and the resource types in each service folder must not duplicate each other, except for operations, locations, checkNameAvailability etc., which RPaaS requires for HTTP request schema validation. Each service-name folder must duplicate the special "list operations" API.
   - Each new control-plane api-version should be unique across all the control-plane service folders of the RP namespace, and a preview and a GA version may never share the same date.
   - Two services may not reference a single shared copy of a contract; if services want to "share" TypeSpec/OpenAPI files, those files must be explicitly copied into each consuming service's folder on its own timeline.
2. If they are not independent services, or if you believe your case needs an exception, send an email to azversioning@service.microsoft.com (the contact alias named in the guideline) to justify your case.

On the RT registration itself: the RPaaS team doesn't require you to specify the RTRegistration down to the sub folder level, it can find the resource types in sub folders recursively according to Lakshman and Wendy who are from the RPaaS team. Which means
```
"azure-rest-api-specs-pr/tree/RPSaaSMaster/specification/identitygovernance/resource-manager/Microsoft.EntraidGovernance/"
```
should work for your scenario, for both the existing resource types and the new ScimApiConsumption one - you do not need to change the existing registration to point at `.../Microsoft.EntraidGovernance/preview`, nor scope the new registration to `.../Microsoft.EntraidGovernance/ScimApiConsumption`. Because the discovery is recursive, it does matter that resource types are not duplicated across the service folders. But I suggest you to carefully verify it in your dogfood or canary environment before you publish it.

query:
title: Questions About Maintaining TypeSpec and Reducing Learning Costs

question: I'm from the MySQL service team. I’ve already migrated the swagger to TypeSpec, but I have two questions and would like to ask if you have any best practices.
1. How do you maintain TypeSpec in parallel?
Here are our common scenarios: we usually have two versions in progress.
For example, the 2025-09-01 version is almost finished — we’re waiting for the backend code to be ready before we can release it, though we may still have some small changes.
Another version, 2025-12-01, has just started. Feature owners are designing their features and want to start merging code into this version.
How can we develop these two versions in parallel? I don’t have permission to create branches.
2. For the server team, each feature owner needs to write their own feature, which means everyone has to understand how to write TypeSpec.
How can we reduce their learning and writing cost?
ground_truth:
1. `don’t have permission to create branches.`
I think this might mean you haven't onboarded to the repo correctly. I would expect this to be the workflow if you need to work on a new version of a non released one to just branch of in the spec repo

query:
title: Understanding what changes after typespec conversion

question: I'm looking for some help in understanding what changes after a service has converted to typespec in terms of releases. I heard that after conversion, the resource provider should discontinue updating swaggers. What does this look like in practice, and what is the new expectation in terms of api version titling?
 
Microsoft.MachineLearningServices has some technical debt where we have been basing new preview versions off the previous preview version, and new stable versions off the previous stable version. With typespec, it seems like new API versions will just require adding remove and add decorators to handle this (until we can move to one track releases). Looking for some help in understanding the basics, thank you!
ground_truth:
Once your service has migrated to TypeSpec, the release and maintenance workflow changes significantly from the legacy Swagger/OpenAPI model. Here’s what you should expect:
1.Discontinuing Swagger Updates: After converting, you must stop maintaining or hand-writing Swagger files. All changes to your service API—new versions, additions, removals—must be done in TypeSpec files. OpenAPI (Swagger) is now a generated artifact from TypeSpec. Any changes required in the OpenAPI output must be made by updating TypeSpec and re-generating, not by editing OpenAPI directly.
2.API Version Titling: API versions in TypeSpec are managed via an enum, usually called `Versions`. Each entry represents a supported API version (e.g., `v2024_06_01_preview: "2024-06-01-preview"`). You title new API versions by adding new entries to this enum. The expectation is that your TypeSpec project maintains a single, unified source of truth for all API versions, with clear version titling.
3.Handling Preview/Stable Branching with Decorators: The old workflow of copying and branching preview/stable .json files is replaced by TypeSpec’s versioning decorators:
Use `@added(VERSION)` to introduce a new property/operation/model in a specific API version.
Use `@removed(VERSION)` to remove something starting with a given version.
These decorators let you express exactly which versions include or omit specific features, so you no longer have to manually copy files or branch spec logic. See the example below:

```
model ResourceProperties {
  /** This property was introduced in preview version */
  @added(Versions.v2024_06_01_preview)
  previewProperty?: string;
  /** This property is removed from stable version */
  @removed(Versions.v2024_08_01)
  legacyProperty?: int32;
}
```

4.Best Practice: Move Toward Single-Track Releases: Azure recommends maintaining only one active preview version at a time (except for ARM retention requirements). When a new preview is published, older previews should be retired, which TypeSpec makes much easier. This minimizes technical debt and confusion.
5.Release Process Changes:
When you need a new API version, update the `Versions` enum and annotate changes using `@added`/`@removed` (and optionally `@renamedFrom`, etc.).
No need to copy-paste or fork files—just annotate differences inline.
Generate OpenAPI/Swagger from TypeSpec for release, but do not edit it by hand.
6.Migration Expectations:
The OpenAPI converter can help with initial migration, but you’ll need to manually adjust TypeSpec for proper versioning, linter compliance, and best practices.
All future API evolution (new features, breaking changes) should use TypeSpec’s versioning system.
Summary:
You maintain only TypeSpec going forward, not Swagger.
API version titling is centralized in a TypeSpec enum.
Preview/stable branching is handled with decorators, not file copies.
Move toward one-track releases for clarity and supportability.
For details and migration guidance, see the references below.
